issues.legal_issue: Property held by a former sovereign was not shown to be joint family property capable of partition.
material_facts: The disputed properties had been held by successive rulers while the holder was sovereign, and the record did not establish that the properties were acquired by or belonged to a family estate.
The claimant produced no title documents or other convincing evidence showing the source of acquisition or a family interest in the disputed properties.
The disputed properties were not included in a detailed family partition, although the family members knew of the properties and carefully described the properties they did partition.
Only the former ruler filed a return in the land-ceiling proceedings, as an individual; other family members did not claim the lands as family property.
The former ruler identified the disputed properties as private property in an inventory submitted under the integration covenant, and the Government of India accepted the inventory.
Documents produced by the former ruler indicated that certain properties were treated as State property before the transfer of sovereignty.
issues.conclusion: The disputed properties were the former ruler’s personal properties, not joint family properties, and the claims for partition and related relief were rightly dismissed.
issues.legal_principle: An absolute sovereign’s will governs the properties held under his sovereignty; municipal family law does not give family members a co-ownership interest by birth in sovereign property. The sovereign may use or dispose of such property as he chooses, and the ordinary distinction between State and private property did not govern the sovereign’s holdings in the same way as it governs ordinary ownership. A claimant asserting that an asset was held in a different capacity must plead and establish that claim. The Court relied on Ameer-un-Nissa Begum v. Mahboob Begum, Director of Endowments v. Akram Ali, Madhavrao Phalke v. State of Madhya Bharat, Tilkoyat Shri Govindlalji Maharaj v. State of Rajasthan, Mangal Singh v. Legal Remembrancer, Punjab, and the principles discussed in D.S. Meramwala Bhayala v. Ba Shri Amarba Jethsurbhai and Vishnu Pratap Singh v. State of Madhya Pradesh. The rules concerning impartible joint family property could assist only if the properties were first shown to be joint family property.

rule.if: appeal_from_partition_suit_dismissal and former_holder_was_absolute_sovereign and no_convincing_evidence_of_family_title and assets_omitted_from_known_family_partition and assets_listed_as_private_and_accepted

predicates.appeal_from_partition_suit_dismissal: The claimant appealed from the dismissal of a suit seeking partition and related relief.
predicates.former_holder_was_absolute_sovereign: The disputed assets were held by a person who exercised absolute sovereign authority over the territory in which they were held.
predicates.no_convincing_evidence_of_family_title: The claimant did not produce convincing evidence establishing that the disputed assets belonged to the family estate.
predicates.assets_omitted_from_known_family_partiti: Family members who knew of the disputed assets omitted them from a detailed partition of the family properties.
predicates.assets_listed_as_private_and_accepted: The former sovereign listed the disputed assets as private property in an inventory submitted during the transfer of sovereignty, and the receiving government accepted the list.

issues.definition: When an appeal from dismissal of a partition suit concerns assets held by an absolute sovereign, and the claimant lacks convincing proof of family title while the assets were omitted from a known family partition and accepted as listed private property, the assets are treated as personal rather than joint family property.

issues.legal_issue: A claim that property constituted a customary separate estate could not be determined when that theory was not pleaded or tried and had been disclaimed in the appeal below.
material_facts: The claimant did not plead that the properties constituted a customary separate estate or that the former ruler held them in the capacity associated with such an estate.
No issue was framed on that theory, and the record did not show that the opposing party went to trial knowing the theory was in issue or produced evidence on that basis.

In the grounds of appeal before the High Court, the claimant had specifically denied that the relevant document created such an estate and denied that the former ruler claimed to hold the properties in that capacity.
issues.conclusion: The claimant could not raise the customary separate-estate theory for the first time on appeal, and the Court did not decide the case on that basis.
issues.legal_principle: Evidence on issues actually tried cannot found a decision on a different issue that was not put in issue and on which the parties had no opportunity to adduce evidence. The rule does not apply where the parties knew that the particular question was in issue and adduced evidence on it despite the absence of a formal issue. Whether a customary separate estate exists depends on evidence of usage and therefore is not a pure question of law that can be introduced without a factual foundation. The Court relied on Siddik Mahomed Shah v. Mt. Saran, Nagubai Ammal v. B. Shama Rao, Moran Mar Basselios Catholicos v. Thukalan Paulo Avira, and the discussion of customary usage in P.R. Sundara Aiyar’s treatise on Malabar and Aliyasanthana law.

rule.if: civil_property_appeal and customary_estate_theory_not_pleaded and no_trial_notice_or_evidence_on_theory and appellant_disclaimed_theory_below

predicates.civil_property_appeal: The matter is an appeal concerning competing claims to property in a civil proceeding.
predicates.customary_estate_theory_not_pleaded: The claimant did not plead that the property was held under a customary separate-estate arrangement.
predicates.no_trial_notice_or_evidence_on_theory: The opposing party did not go to trial with notice that the customary-estate question was in issue, and the parties did not adduce evidence on that question.
predicates.appellant_disclaimed_theory_below: The claimant expressly denied the customary-estate theory in the grounds of appeal before the intermediate appellate court.

issues.definition: When a civil property appeal introduces an unpleaded customary-estate theory that was not tried with notice and evidence and was disclaimed below, the theory is not considered.

issues.legal_issue: Statutory rules governing interests in family property did not apply to assets found to be the former ruler’s personal property.
material_facts: The Court found that the disputed properties were the former ruler’s personal properties rather than properties of a family estate.
The claimant relied on statutory rules concerning devolution of interests in family property and the conversion of joint-family holdings into holdings in common.
The conditions for applying those rules depended on the assets being family property or joint family property.
issues.conclusion: The statutory provisions relied on by the claimant did not apply to the disputed properties, and they did not transform the former ruler’s personal property into joint family property.
issues.legal_principle: Section 7(1) of the Hindu Succession Act, 1956 applies to an interest in property of a tarwad, tavazhi, or illom. Section 4(2) of the Kerala Joint Hindu Family System (Abolition) Act, 1975 applies to members of a qualifying joint Hindu family holding joint family property when that Act came into force. Neither provision applies where the property is personal property rather than property of the relevant family kind. The Court therefore did not need to decide whether statutory changes would make otherwise joint but impartible property partible.

predicates.appeal_concerning_partition_or_family_pr: The proceeding seeks partition or relies on legal rules governing interests in family property.
predicates.assets_found_to_be_personal_property: The disputed assets were found to belong personally to the holder rather than to a family estate.

issues.definition: When a partition or family-property proceeding concerns assets found to be personal property, statutory rules that require family property as their basis do not apply to those assets.
